name: Grangemouth
desc: Commercial port. A visiting sailing yacht asking FTNS for a berth should usually be pointed at the Visitor berths filter, not here.
body:
Not a visitor yacht berth. If FTNS is asked for a leisure night alongside, do not send the yacht here — use the Visitor berths filter and point them at Granton, Port Edgar or a small harbour.

Scotland’s largest port and the country’s principal container and reefer terminal. Cargo moving through Grangemouth is estimated to represent around 30% of Scottish GDP.

Specialist terminals handle containers, clean oils, chemicals, LPG and general cargo. Seven weekly feeder services connect the port to European and deep-sea hubs used by the world’s top shipping lines.

The site sits inside the Forth Green Freeport and is rail-linked to both East and West Coast main lines, with around 600,000 sq ft of warehousing and a 775 m rail siding.
facts:
Throughput ~ 9 Mt / year
Containers ~ 250k+ TEU
Trade value ~ £6 bn / year
Reach ~ 70% of Scotland < 1 hr

name: Bo'ness
desc: Visitor berth candidate. FTNS can send a leisure yacht here instead of a commercial Forth Ports dock — confirm availability with the harbour or club first.
body:
Bo’ness (Borrowstounness) sits on the south shore of the upper Forth. The historic harbour is now primarily leisure and heritage-oriented rather than a deep-water commercial terminal.

The town is better known for the Bo’ness & Kinneil Railway and the nearby Kinneil House than for freight. Commercial traffic on this stretch of the firth is concentrated at Grangemouth a few miles west.

For a visiting yacht, this is a possible leisure stop — not Grangemouth. Confirm depth, drying and contact before sending anyone here.
facts:
Status ~ Small harbour
Note ~ Not a Forth Ports commercial dock

name: Crombie
desc: Commercial port. A visiting sailing yacht asking FTNS for a berth should usually be pointed at the Visitor berths filter, not here.
body: Crombie Jetty is a deep-water jetty on the north shore of the Firth of Forth near Rosyth, Fife. Historically associated with naval and industrial operations, it has supported the movement of fuel and bulk cargoes due to its strategic location and marine access. Today, it remains a notable feature of the Forth's maritime infrastructure and heritage.
facts:
Status ~ Private Jetty
Note ~ Not to be used for leisure

name: Braefoot Terminal
desc: Commercial port. A visiting sailing yacht asking FTNS for a berth should usually be pointed at the Visitor berths filter, not here.
body: Braefoot Bay Oil Terminal is located on the north shore of the Firth of Forth near Dalgety Bay, Fife. The terminal serves as a key import and distribution facility for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), receiving cargoes from international tankers via its deep-water jetty. Due to its strategic location and specialist infrastructure, Braefoot Bay plays an important role in Scotland's energy supply network and is a prominent feature of the Forth's industrial waterfront.
facts: Note ~ Not to be used for leisure

name: Rosyth
desc: Commercial port. A visiting sailing yacht asking FTNS for a berth should usually be pointed at the Visitor berths filter, not here.
body:
Not a casual visitor yacht berth. Commercial, cruise, agri and defence traffic. A visiting leisure yacht looking for a night’s rest should be sent to Port Edgar, immediately east under the bridges — not into this dock.

Forth Ports Rosyth sits on the north bank of the Forth, immediately west of the Forth Bridges, with deep-water river berths and the only ro-ro berth on Scotland’s east coast (floating linkspan, all-tide access).

It has grown into a cruise turnaround hub and Scotland’s premier agri-feed hub, while remaining important for project cargo, automotive and defence mobilisation. The adjacent historic dockyard (Babcock) still supports naval work.

North Wall offers a long deep-water frontage and heavy-lift cranage. The port is upstream of the bridges but can take deep-sea vessels.
facts:
Berths ~ 6 working berths
Cargo ~ 250-550 kt / year
Depth ~ 8 m MLWS (N. Wall)
Road ~ 2 miles for M90

name: South Queensferry / Hound Point
desc: Commercial port. A visiting sailing yacht asking FTNS for a berth should usually be pointed at the Visitor berths filter, not here.
body:
South Queensferry is the historic ferry crossing under the Forth Bridge. Commercial shipping interest here is dominated by Hound Point, the deep-water crude oil terminal just east of the bridges on the south shore.

Hound Point loads North Sea crude from the Forties pipeline system onto tankers (typically Aframax / Panamax class). It is one of two specialised oil & gas marine terminals in the Forth managed within the Forth Ports statutory harbour area.

The village itself is a visitor gateway to the three Forth bridges rather than a working cargo port.
facts:
Hound Point ~ Panamax crude terminal
Operator ~ Ineos / Forth system
Note ~ Not a general cargo port

name: Leith (Edinburgh)
desc: Commercial port. A visiting sailing yacht asking FTNS for a berth should usually be pointed at the Visitor berths filter, not here.
body:
Usually the wrong answer for a visiting sailing yacht. Leith is an enclosed commercial port. Cost, security and working traffic make it a poor first suggestion. FTNS should point leisure arrivals at Granton (RFYC / FCYC / Edinburgh Marina pontoon) or Port Edgar instead.

Scotland’s largest enclosed deep-water port, on the south shore immediately north-east of Edinburgh. It can accept ships up to about 50,000 DWT and has two dry docks plus extensive inner basins.

Leith is the capital’s cruise gateway (and home berth of the Royal Yacht Britannia) and a growing renewables / offshore-wind marshalling and manufacturing site, including the Charles Hammond deep-water berth and a large Freeport tax site.

Cargo includes dry bulk, project cargo, agri-products, pipes and decommissioning work. Large cruise ships often use Forth anchorages and tender to Newhaven when the enclosed docks are constrained.
facts:
Max ship ~50,000 DWT
Quayage ~ 4,000 m+ internal
Cargo >1 Mt / year
City ~ 3 miles from centre

name: Burntisland
desc: Commercial port. A visiting sailing yacht asking FTNS for a berth should usually be pointed at the Visitor berths filter, not here.
body:
One of the Forth’s oldest natural harbours, on the Fife shore opposite Leith. Forth Ports operates it as a Fife satellite port for dry bulk, breakbulk, paper & forest products, oil & gas support and offshore renewables.

Burntisland Fabrications (BiFab) and Briggs Marine are long-standing tenants. The harbour is being positioned, with Leith, as a Mid-Forth pair for offshore-wind marshalling and component assembly under the Forth Green Freeport.
facts:
Character ~ Oldest natural harbour on the Forth
Tenants ~ Bifab, Briggs Marine
Role ~ Fife satellite port

name: Kirkcaldy
desc: Commercial port. A visiting sailing yacht asking FTNS for a berth should usually be pointed at the Visitor berths filter, not here.
body:
Kirkcaldy Harbour on the north Forth handles standard general-cargo coasters, with a particular strength in grains and cereals. It reopened to commercial traffic in 2011 after a long gap.

Together with Burntisland and Methil it forms Forth Ports’ Fife satellite cluster — smaller than Grangemouth or Leith but useful for regional bulk and agri cargoes
facts:
Reopened ~ 2011 (commercial)
Typical ~ Coaster-sized vessels
Role ~ Fife satellite port

name: Methil
desc: Commercial port. A visiting sailing yacht asking FTNS for a berth should usually be pointed at the Visitor berths filter, not here.
body:
The most easterly of the Fife ports, Methil has two docks and specialises in timber, wood pulp, aggregates, grain and general bulk. It is a national distribution point for timber merchants.

Around 50 acres of development land and an energy / renewables hinterland make it relevant to decommissioning and offshore support as well as traditional bulk trades.
facts:
Docks ~ Two docks
Max ~ 3,000 DWT typical
Land ~ 50 acres development

name: North Berwick
desc: Visitor berth candidate. FTNS can send a leisure yacht here instead of a commercial Forth Ports dock — confirm availability with the harbour or club first.
body:
A small East Lothian harbour used by fishing boats, trip vessels to Bass Rock and the Isle of May, and leisure craft. It is not a commercial freight port.

East Lothian Yacht Club races off this harbour and hosts the open and keelboat regattas. On those weekends the harbour is a racing base as well as a working haven — see the ELYC pins on the Clubs and Races layers.

The town is a visitor centre for the outer Forth’s seabird colonies; Bass Rock is one of the world’s largest gannetries.
facts:
Use ~ Harbour & marina
Landmark ~ Bass rock offshore

name: Dunbar
desc: Visitor berth candidate. FTNS can send a leisure yacht here instead of a commercial Forth Ports dock — confirm availability with the harbour or club first.
body: Historic fishing harbour on the East Lothian coast at the eastern edge of this chart extract. Still a working harbour for inshore boats and leisure traffic rather than deep-sea cargo.
facts:
Use ~ Working harbour
Coast ~ Eastern limit of this chart

name: Anstruther
desc: Visitor berth candidate. FTNS can send a leisure yacht here instead of a commercial Forth Ports dock — confirm availability with the harbour or club first.
body:
Principal harbour of the East Neuk of Fife. Traditionally a herring port, now a mix of inshore fishing, creel boats and visitor traffic. The Scottish Fisheries Museum sits on the harbour.

Also a destination for Forth passage races and cruises-in-company from Granton. Those weekends are when a small harbour most needs a card that the arriving club, not a central team, has written.
facts:
Use ~ Fisheries & visitor harbour
Region ~ East Neuk of Fife

name: Inverkeithing
desc: Commercial port. A visiting sailing yacht asking FTNS for a berth should usually be pointed at the Visitor berths filter, not here.
body: A small Fife harbour immediately east of Rosyth. Inverkeithing was once one of Britain’s best-known shipbreaking yards (Thos. W. Ward). Today it is a minor harbour in the shadow of the commercial and naval facilities at Rosyth.
facts:
Nearby ~ Rosyth / Forth Bridges
History ~ Famous shipbreaking yard

name: Queensferry
body: Queensferry is a historic coastal town situated on the southern shore of the Firth of Forth. Renowned for its maritime heritage and stunning views of the iconic Forth Bridges, it remains an important centre for tourism, leisure boating, and ferry services, while retaining its strong connection to Scotland’s seafaring history.

name: Granton
body: Granton Harbour is a historic harbour on the Firth of Forth in Edinburgh. Once an important commercial port, it now supports leisure boating, marine activities, and forms part of the ongoing regeneration of the Granton waterfront.

name: Newhaven Harbour
body: Newhaven is a historic harbour district located on the northern coast of Edinburgh, on the Firth of Forth. Traditionally a fishing and maritime community, it remains a popular destination for leisure boating, local seafood, and waterfront recreation, while continuing to play a role in the area's ongoing coastal development.
